purpose: Manual Grammar QG bench expansion: extend the P14 production-candidate bench from 110 to 188 template families before any further generator-only certification work.
sourceBoundary: Authored as a separate draft content-bench line after P14. Not yet integrated into worker/src/subjects/grammar/content.js.

targetAfterIntegration.minimumIntegrationRequirement: Each new template family must ship with at least 2 hand-authored fixed cases and an expansion path to 6+ learner-visible surfaces before production certification.

templates.title: Direct and indirect questions
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence is a direct question that needs a question mark?
cases.correct: Can the library open early today?
cases.explanation: A direct question asks the reader/listener something directly.
options: Can the library open early today?
Aisha wondered whether the library could open early.
The library can open early today.
How useful it would be if the library opened early

cases.prompt: Which sentence is an indirect question and should end with a full stop?
cases.correct: Dad asked whether the train had arrived.
cases.explanation: It reports a question, but the whole sentence is a statement.
options: Dad asked whether the train had arrived.

templates.title: Polite commands and requests
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence is a command, even though it sounds polite?
cases.explanation: A command tells someone to do something; 'please' does not stop it being a command.
options: Could you pass the glue stick?
The glue stick is on the table.
What a useful glue stick this is!

cases.prompt: Which sentence is a question, not a command?
cases.explanation: It asks something and needs a question mark.
options: Close the window before the rain comes.

templates.title: Grammatical exclamation vs excited statement
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence is a grammatical exclamation?
cases.correct: What a fierce storm that was!
cases.explanation: In KS2 grammar, an exclamation often starts with 'What' or 'How' and contains a verb.
options: What a fierce storm that was!
The storm knocked over the bins!

cases.prompt: Which sentence is an excited statement, not a grammatical exclamation?
cases.explanation: It tells us something; the exclamation mark alone does not make it a grammatical exclamation.
options: What a brilliant race that was!

templates.title: Sentence function classification in context
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Classify each sentence: statement, question, command or exclamation.
cases.explanation: Use the job of the whole sentence, not only its final punctuation.
rows: The baker opened the shop at six.
What a busy shop this is!

cases.prompt: Classify each sentence: statement, question, command or exclamation.
cases.explanation: Look at whether the sentence tells, asks, instructs or exclaims.
rows: Could the artist paint another picture?

templates.title: Same word, different word class
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: In 'The children will light the lantern', what word class is 'light'?
cases.explanation: Here, 'light' is the action being done.

cases.prompt: In 'The light rain stopped after lunch', what word class is 'light'?
cases.explanation: Here, 'light' describes the noun 'rain'.

templates.title: Determiner or pronoun in context
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: In 'Those are my boots', what word class is 'Those'?
cases.explanation: It stands in for a noun phrase.

cases.prompt: In 'Those boots are muddy', what word class is 'Those'?
cases.explanation: It comes before the noun 'boots' and helps identify it.

templates.title: Adverbs modifying adjectives and clauses
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: In 'The soup was almost cold', what word class is 'almost'?
cases.explanation: It modifies the adjective 'cold'.

cases.prompt: In 'Luckily, the gate was still open', what word class is 'Luckily'?
cases.explanation: It comments on the whole clause.

templates.title: Preposition versus conjunction
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: In 'After the match, we ate sandwiches', what word class is 'After'?
cases.explanation: It introduces the phrase 'the match', not a clause.

cases.prompt: In 'After the match ended, we ate sandwiches', what word class is 'After'?
cases.explanation: It introduces the clause 'the match ended'.

templates.title: Multi-select word class identification
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Select all the determiners: 'The small boat crossed a wide river near those trees.'
cases.explanation: Determiners help identify nouns.

cases.prompt: Select all the prepositions: 'Before breakfast, Maya placed the bag under the bench.'
cases.explanation: Prepositions show time or place relationships here.

templates.title: Find the head noun
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: In 'the cracked blue bowl on the shelf', which word is the head noun?
cases.explanation: The noun phrase is centred on 'bowl'.

cases.prompt: In 'a narrow path through the woods', which word is the head noun?
cases.explanation: The main noun being described is 'path'.

templates.title: Noun phrase versus clause
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which option is a noun phrase, not a clause?
cases.correct: the silver watch in the drawer
cases.explanation: A noun phrase centres on a noun and does not contain a finite verb as a clause does.
options: the silver watch in the drawer

cases.prompt: Which option is a clause, not a noun phrase?
cases.explanation: A clause contains a subject and verb.
options: a watch with a cracked face
the old watch on the desk

templates.title: Expand a noun phrase with a preposition phrase
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Add words to make an expanded noun phrase: 'the fox ___'.
cases.correct: the fox beside the old wall
cases.explanation: The added words should stay attached to the noun, not turn it into a full clause.
accepted: the fox beside the old wall

cases.prompt: Add words to make an expanded noun phrase: 'a key ___'.
cases.explanation: The phrase is still centred on the noun 'key'.
accepted: a key with a brass tag

templates.title: Repair an overgrown noun phrase
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which revision keeps only the noun phrase? 'the old dog that barked at the postman'
cases.correct: the old dog by the gate
cases.explanation: The correct choice is a phrase, not a clause.
options: the old dog by the gate
the old dog barked at the postman
the dog was old and loud

cases.prompt: Which option is a clear expanded noun phrase?
cases.correct: the cracked mirror in the hall
cases.explanation: It has a noun with extra detail attached.
options: the cracked mirror in the hall
because the mirror was in the hall

templates.title: Determiner and modifier order
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which noun phrase has a sensible determiner-adjective-noun order?
cases.explanation: Determiner first, then modifiers, then noun.

cases.prompt: Which option is a well-formed noun phrase?
cases.explanation: 'Those' works as a determiner before the noun phrase.

templates.title: Classify adverbials by function
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Classify each adverbial as when, where or how.
cases.explanation: Adverbials can tell when, where or how something happens.

cases.prompt: Classify each adverbial as when, where or how.
cases.explanation: Ask what information the phrase adds to the verb or clause.

templates.title: Move an adverbial to the front
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Rewrite with the adverbial at the front: 'The team practised before the final.'
cases.correct: Before the final, the team practised.
cases.explanation: A fronted adverbial normally takes a comma in these KS2 questions.
accepted: Before the final, the team practised.
nearMiss: Before the final the team practised.

cases.prompt: Rewrite with the adverbial at the front: 'Maya waited beside the oak tree.'
cases.correct: Beside the oak tree, Maya waited.
cases.explanation: Move the place adverbial to the beginning and add a comma.
accepted: Beside the oak tree, Maya waited.
nearMiss: Beside the oak tree Maya waited.

templates.title: Not every opener is a fronted adverbial
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence starts with a fronted adverbial?
cases.explanation: The opening phrase tells us when.

cases.prompt: Which sentence does NOT begin with a fronted adverbial?
cases.correct: The market opened early in the morning.
cases.explanation: The adverbial is at the end, not fronted.
options: In the morning, the market opened early.
The market opened early in the morning.
With a smile, the seller waved.

templates.title: Fronted adverbial comma precision
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
cases.correct: At the edge of the field, the horses waited.
cases.explanation: The comma follows the whole fronted adverbial.
options: At the edge of the field the horses waited.
At the edge, of the field the horses waited.
At the edge of the field, the horses waited.
At, the edge of the field the horses waited.

cases.prompt: Which sentence places the comma after the fronted adverbial?
cases.correct: During the storm, the lights flickered.
cases.explanation: The whole phrase 'During the storm' is fronted.
options: During, the storm the lights flickered.
During the storm, the lights flickered.
During the storm the, lights flickered.
During the storm the lights, flickered.

templates.title: Main and subordinate clauses
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Classify each clause.
cases.explanation: A main clause can stand alone; a subordinate clause depends on another clause.

cases.prompt: Classify each clause.
cases.explanation: Look for subordinating conjunctions such as when, if and because.
rows: the candles are in the drawer

templates.title: Choose a conjunction for meaning
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which conjunction best combines the ideas? 'The pitch was wet. The match continued.'
cases.explanation: The second idea contrasts with the first.

cases.prompt: Which conjunction best shows cause? 'We stayed inside. The rain was heavy.'
cases.explanation: The heavy rain explains why we stayed inside.

templates.title: Repair a subordinate-clause fragment
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which revision makes this fragment a complete sentence? 'Because the gate was locked.'
cases.correct: Because the gate was locked, we climbed over the stile.
cases.explanation: A subordinate clause needs a main clause.
options: Because the gate was locked, we climbed over the stile.

cases.prompt: Which sentence fixes the fragment? 'Although the team was tired.'
cases.correct: Although the team was tired, they finished the match.
cases.explanation: The main clause completes the meaning.
options: Although the team was tired, they finished the match.

templates.title: Combine clauses with precise punctuation
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Combine using 'although': 'Lena was nervous. She read her poem clearly.'
cases.correct: Although Lena was nervous, she read her poem clearly.
cases.explanation: Use both ideas and punctuate the fronted subordinate clause.
accepted: Although Lena was nervous, she read her poem clearly.
Lena read her poem clearly although she was nervous.

cases.prompt: Combine using 'because': 'The ground was frozen. We could not dig the hole.'
cases.correct: We could not dig the hole because the ground was frozen.
cases.explanation: Because shows the cause.
accepted: We could not dig the hole because the ground was frozen.
Because the ground was frozen, we could not dig the hole.

templates.title: Clause boundary or phrase
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which option is a subordinate clause?
cases.explanation: It has a subject and verb introduced by 'when'.
options: a lantern with a cracked handle

cases.prompt: Which option is a phrase, not a clause?
cases.explanation: It has no finite verb.

templates.title: Identify relative pronouns
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which word introduces the relative clause? 'The climber who reached the top waved.'
cases.explanation: 'Who' introduces extra information about the climber.

cases.prompt: Which word introduces the relative clause? 'The path that led to the beach was steep.'
cases.explanation: 'That' links the clause to the noun 'path'.

templates.title: Relative clause versus time clause
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence contains a relative clause?
cases.correct: The hall where we practise is closed today.
cases.explanation: 'Where we practise' gives information about the hall.
options: When we practise, the hall is noisy.
The hall where we practise is closed today.
We practise in the hall after school.
Because the hall is closed, we practise outside.

cases.prompt: Which sentence contains a time clause, not a relative clause?
cases.correct: When the museum opened, the class went inside.
cases.explanation: 'When the museum opened' tells us time.
options: The museum that we visited was busy.
The guide who met us smiled.
When the museum opened, the class went inside.
The room where we waited was cold.

templates.title: Commas for non-defining relative clauses
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
cases.correct: Mr Patel, who teaches Year 6, runs chess club.
cases.explanation: The extra information is parenthetical and needs paired commas.
options: Mr Patel who teaches Year 6, runs chess club.
Mr Patel, who teaches Year 6, runs chess club.
Mr Patel who teaches, Year 6 runs chess club.
Mr Patel, who teaches Year 6 runs, chess club.

cases.prompt: Which sentence correctly punctuates the extra information?
cases.correct: The River Dee, which flows through Chester, flooded last winter.
cases.explanation: The relative clause is extra information.
options: The River Dee which flows through Chester, flooded last winter.
The River Dee, which flows through Chester, flooded last winter.
The River Dee, which flows, through Chester flooded last winter.
The River Dee which, flows through Chester, flooded last winter.

templates.title: Complete with a relative clause
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Complete the sentence: 'The scientist ___ explained the experiment.'
cases.explanation: The clause adds information about the scientist.

cases.prompt: Complete the sentence: 'The painting ___ was sold at auction.'
cases.correct: that hung in the school hall
cases.explanation: The relative clause links to 'painting'.
options: that hung in the school hall
and it hung in the hall

templates.title: Present perfect in context
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence uses the present perfect?
cases.explanation: Present perfect uses has/have + past participle and links to now.
options: Maya had finished her model before lunch.

cases.prompt: Which sentence should use the present perfect? 'The bus is here now because it ___.'
cases.explanation: The result matters now.

templates.title: Past perfect sequence
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Choose the best verb form: 'By the time Dad called, I ___ the homework.'
cases.explanation: Past perfect shows one past action happened before another past action.

cases.prompt: Choose the best verb form: 'The birds flew away because the cat ___ too close.'
cases.explanation: The creeping happened before the birds flew away.

templates.title: Progressive forms with interruption
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Choose the best form: 'We ___ the fence when the rain started.'
cases.explanation: Past progressive shows an action in progress.

cases.prompt: Choose the best form: 'The dog ___ under the table while we ate.'
cases.explanation: It was happening over a period of time in the past.

templates.title: Rewrite while preserving meaning
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Rewrite in the past perfect: 'She leaves before the bell.'
cases.correct: She had left before the bell.
cases.explanation: Use had + past participle.
accepted: She had left before the bell.

cases.prompt: Rewrite in the present perfect: 'They clean the classroom.'
cases.explanation: Use have + past participle.

templates.title: Classify tense/aspect
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Classify each verb phrase.
cases.explanation: Look at the auxiliary verbs.

cases.prompt: Classify each verb phrase.
cases.explanation: Progressive uses be + -ing; perfect uses have/had + past participle.

templates.title: Standard was/were agreement
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Choose the Standard English form: 'We ___ waiting by the gate.'
cases.explanation: 'We were' is the Standard English form.

cases.prompt: Choose the Standard English form: 'They ___ excited about the trip.'
cases.explanation: Use 'were' with they.

templates.title: Did/done in Standard English
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence uses Standard English?
cases.correct: I did my homework before tea.
cases.explanation: 'Did' is the correct past-tense form here.
options: I done my homework before tea.
I did my homework before tea.
I doing my homework before tea.

cases.prompt: Which correction is best? 'She done the washing up.'
cases.explanation: Use 'did' in Standard English.
options: She done did the washing up.

templates.title: Avoid double negatives
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence is Standard English?
cases.explanation: Standard English does not use 'no' after 'haven't' in this way.

cases.prompt: Choose the Standard English correction: 'There isn't no milk left.'
cases.explanation: Use 'any' with the negative verb.

templates.title: Formal subject-verb agreement
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Choose the Standard English form: 'The group of pupils ___ ready.'
cases.explanation: The subject is singular: 'group'.

cases.prompt: Choose the Standard English form: 'Neither of the answers ___ correct.'
cases.explanation: 'Neither' is treated as singular in this formal sentence.

templates.title: Clear pronoun reference
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence keeps the meaning clearest?
cases.correct: Sara gave the book to Lily because Lily needed it.
cases.explanation: Repeating 'Lily' avoids ambiguity.
options: Sara gave the book to Lily because she needed it.
Sara gave the book to Lily because Lily needed it.
She gave it to her because she needed it.
Sara gave Lily to the book because it needed her.

cases.prompt: Which version avoids an unclear pronoun?
cases.correct: Tom put the mug on the tray because the tray was clean.
cases.explanation: 'It' could refer to mug or tray.
options: Tom put the mug on the tray because it was clean.
Tom put the mug on the tray because the tray was clean.
He put it on it because it was clean.
The tray put Tom on the mug.

templates.title: Reduce repetition without losing meaning
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which version improves cohesion?
cases.correct: Mila packed her bag and carried it to the bus.
cases.explanation: The pronouns are clear and avoid repetition.
options: Mila packed Mila's bag and carried Mila's bag to the bus.
Mila packed her bag and carried it to the bus.
Mila packed it and carried her to the bus.
She packed her and carried it to it.

cases.prompt: Which sentence uses pronouns clearly?
cases.correct: Arun found his coat and hung it on the peg.
cases.explanation: 'His' and 'it' have clear referents.
options: Arun found Arun's coat and hung Arun's coat on the peg.
Arun found his coat and hung it on the peg.
Arun found it and hung him on the peg.
He found his and hung it on him.

templates.title: Repair ambiguous pronouns
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Rewrite to make the meaning clear: 'Aisha told Grace she had won the prize.' Make Aisha the winner.
cases.correct: Aisha told Grace that Aisha had won the prize.
cases.explanation: Repeat the noun or restructure the sentence.
accepted: Aisha told Grace that Aisha had won the prize.
Aisha, who had won the prize, told Grace.
nearMiss: Aisha told Grace she had won the prize.

cases.prompt: Rewrite to make the meaning clear: 'The cup hit the plate and it cracked.' Make the plate cracked.
cases.correct: The cup hit the plate, and the plate cracked.
cases.explanation: Avoid the unclear pronoun 'it'.
accepted: The cup hit the plate, and the plate cracked.
When the cup hit the plate, the plate cracked.
nearMiss: The cup hit the plate and it cracked.

templates.title: Choose the clearest referent
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: For each sentence, choose what the pronoun refers to.
cases.explanation: Check which noun makes sense with the action.
rows: Leah fed the rabbit and put it back in the hutch.
Leah put the carrot beside the rabbit and it ate quickly.

cases.prompt: For each sentence, choose what the pronoun refers to.
cases.explanation: Some pronouns are unclear and need rewriting.
rows: The boat struck the rock and it cracked.
The rock cracked after the boat struck it.

templates.title: Formal vocabulary choices
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Choose the most formal replacement for 'find out'.
cases.explanation: 'Discover' is more formal and precise.

cases.prompt: Choose the most formal replacement for 'put off'.
cases.explanation: 'Postpone' suits formal writing.

templates.title: Repair informal sentences
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence is most suitable for a formal letter?
cases.correct: I am writing to request further information.
cases.explanation: Formal writing avoids slang and chatty phrasing.
options: Can you tell me some things?
I am writing to request further information.

cases.prompt: Choose the formal version.
cases.correct: The meeting will take place at 3 p.m.
cases.explanation: It uses precise vocabulary and avoids contractions.
options: The meeting will take place at 3 p.m.

templates.title: Contractions and formal tone
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence is most formal?
cases.correct: The committee cannot approve the request today.
cases.explanation: Formal writing usually avoids contractions.
options: The committee can't approve the request today.
The committee cannot approve the request today.
The committee ain't approving it today.

cases.prompt: Which version best suits a school report?
cases.correct: The experiment did not produce a clear result.
cases.explanation: It is precise and formal.
options: The experiment did not produce a clear result.
The test was kind of useless.

templates.title: Match register to context
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Classify each phrase as formal or informal.
cases.explanation: Formal vocabulary is more precise and less conversational.

cases.prompt: Classify each phrase as formal or informal.
cases.explanation: Consider the setting and audience.

templates.title: Identify passive voice
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence is passive?
cases.correct: The window was broken by the football.
cases.explanation: Passive foregrounds the affected thing: the window.
options: The window was broken by the football.

cases.prompt: Which sentence is active?
cases.explanation: The doer, the council, is the subject.
options: The bridge was repaired by the council.

templates.title: Convert active to passive
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Rewrite in the passive: 'The gardener planted the roses.'
cases.correct: The roses were planted by the gardener.
cases.explanation: Move the object to the front and use was/were + past participle.
accepted: The roses were planted by the gardener.
nearMiss: The gardener was planted by the roses.

cases.prompt: Rewrite in the passive: 'The class will perform the play.'
cases.correct: The play will be performed by the class.
cases.explanation: Keep the future tense with 'will be'.
accepted: The play will be performed by the class.
nearMiss: The class will be performed by the play.

templates.title: Convert passive to active
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Rewrite in the active: 'The trophy was lifted by the captain.'
cases.explanation: The doer becomes the subject.

cases.prompt: Rewrite in the active: 'The song was written by the choir.'
cases.explanation: Keep the meaning the same.

templates.title: Passive voice with hidden agent
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence is passive even though the doer is not named?
cases.correct: The door was locked before lunch.
cases.explanation: Passive can hide the doer.
options: The door was locked before lunch.
The key turned in the lock.

cases.prompt: Which passive sentence leaves out the agent?
cases.correct: The letters were delivered this morning.
cases.explanation: The sentence does not say who delivered them.
options: The letters were delivered this morning.

templates.title: Preserve meaning when changing voice
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which passive sentence keeps the same meaning as 'The dog chased the cat'?
cases.correct: The cat was chased by the dog.
cases.explanation: The cat receives the action.
options: The dog was chased by the cat.
The cat was chased by the dog.
The dog was chasing the cat.

cases.prompt: Which active sentence keeps the same meaning as 'The cake was eaten by Sam'?
cases.explanation: The doer is Sam and the thing affected is the cake.
options: Sam was eaten by the cake.

templates.title: Subject/object with fronted adverbials
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: In 'After dinner, the twins washed the plates', what is the subject?
cases.explanation: Ignore the fronted adverbial; the twins do the action.

cases.prompt: In 'Before sunrise, the hikers packed their tents', what is the object?
cases.explanation: The tents receive the action.

templates.title: Object or complement
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence has a direct object?
cases.explanation: The soup receives the action of tasting.

cases.prompt: Which sentence has no object?
cases.explanation: 'Exhausted' describes the subject; it is not an object.

templates.title: Roles in passive sentences
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: In 'The parcel was delivered by Nina', what is the grammatical subject?
cases.explanation: In a passive sentence, the affected thing can be the subject.

cases.prompt: In 'The windows were cleaned by the caretaker', who is the doer?
cases.explanation: The doer appears in the 'by' phrase.

templates.title: Pronouns as objects
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: In 'Mum called him after school', what is the object?
cases.explanation: 'Him' receives the action.

cases.prompt: In 'The coach praised us', what is the object?
cases.explanation: 'Us' is the pronoun object.

templates.title: Modal certainty scale
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence sounds most certain?
cases.explanation: 'Will' is strongest here.

cases.prompt: Which sentence shows the least certainty?
cases.explanation: 'Might' suggests possibility, not certainty.

templates.title: Obligation and advice
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which modal verb best shows obligation? 'You ___ wear a seat belt.'
cases.explanation: 'Must' shows strong obligation.

cases.prompt: Which modal verb best shows advice? 'You ___ check your work.'
cases.explanation: 'Should' gives advice.

templates.title: Modal verbs and possibility adverbs
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which word is the modal verb? 'Perhaps the concert might be cancelled.'
cases.explanation: 'Might' is the modal verb; 'perhaps' is an adverb.

cases.prompt: Which sentence uses a modal verb to show possibility?
cases.explanation: 'Could' is a modal verb.

templates.title: Choose the best modal for context
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Choose the best modal: 'The clouds are very dark, so it ___ rain soon.'
cases.explanation: There is a possibility, not certainty.

cases.prompt: Choose the best modal: 'The sign says visitors ___ not feed the animals.'
cases.explanation: The sign gives a rule.

templates.title: Identify parenthesis
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which words are parenthesis? 'The bakery, which opens at seven, sells fresh rolls.'
cases.explanation: The words add extra information and can be removed.

cases.prompt: Which part is parenthesis? 'Sam - our team captain - scored twice.'
cases.explanation: The dashes mark extra information.

templates.title: Insert paired commas
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence uses paired commas correctly?
cases.correct: The old mill, now a museum, stands by the river.
cases.explanation: Both sides of the parenthesis need marking.
options: The old mill now, a museum, stands by the river.
The old mill, now a museum, stands by the river.
The old mill, now a museum stands, by the river.
The old, mill now a museum, stands by the river.

cases.prompt: Which sentence marks the parenthesis correctly?
cases.correct: Luca, who had lost his map, asked for help.
cases.explanation: The relative clause is extra information.
options: Luca who had lost his map, asked for help.
Luca, who had lost his map, asked for help.
Luca, who had lost, his map asked for help.
Luca who, had lost his map, asked for help.

templates.title: Parenthesis comma or list comma
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence uses commas for a list, not parenthesis?
cases.correct: We packed torches, maps, ropes and water.
cases.explanation: The commas separate items in a list.
options: We packed torches, maps, ropes and water.
The guide, who knew the cave, led us in.
Ella, our captain, gave the signal.
The cave, dark and cold, stretched ahead.

cases.prompt: Which sentence uses commas for parenthesis?
cases.correct: The violin, a family treasure, was kept in a case.
cases.explanation: 'A family treasure' is extra information.
options: The violin, a family treasure, was kept in a case.
We heard violins, flutes, drums and bells.
The violin sounded clear, bright and loud.
She packed a violin, bow and music stand.

templates.title: Choose punctuation for parenthesis
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which punctuation could replace the brackets? 'The castle (built in 1200) overlooks the town.'
cases.explanation: Dashes or paired commas can mark parenthesis.

cases.prompt: Which sentence uses dashes for parenthesis correctly?
cases.correct: The pond - frozen solid - glittered in the sun.
cases.explanation: The dashes surround the extra information.
options: The pond - frozen solid - glittered in the sun.
The pond - frozen solid glittered - in the sun.
The pond frozen - solid - glittered in the sun.
The pond frozen solid - glittered - in the sun.

templates.title: Question mark inside speech marks
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Punctuate the direct speech: 'Where is my scarf asked Dad.'
cases.explanation: The question mark belongs inside the speech marks.

cases.prompt: Punctuate the direct speech: 'Are we nearly there asked Leila.'
cases.explanation: The spoken question needs the question mark inside the closing speech mark.

templates.title: Reporting clause before speech
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Punctuate: 'Mum whispered the baby is asleep.'
cases.explanation: Use a comma before the direct speech.

cases.prompt: Punctuate: 'The coach shouted run faster.'
cases.explanation: The reporting clause comes before the speech.

templates.title: Split direct speech
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence punctuates split speech correctly?
cases.correct: “We can try again,” said Tom, “after lunch.”
cases.explanation: Commas separate the reporting clause from the speech.
options: “We can try again,” said Tom, “after lunch.”
“We can try again” said Tom “after lunch.”
“We can try again,” said Tom “after lunch.”
“We can try again”, said Tom, “after lunch”.

cases.prompt: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
cases.correct: “I found the key,” whispered Zara, “under the mat.”
cases.explanation: The punctuation stays inside the speech marks.
options: “I found the key,” whispered Zara, “under the mat.”
“I found the key” whispered Zara, “under the mat.”
“I found the key,” whispered Zara “under the mat.”
“I found the key”, whispered Zara, “under the mat”.

templates.title: New speaker, new line
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which layout is clearest when a new person speaks?
cases.correct: Start a new line for the new speaker.
cases.explanation: A new speaker usually starts a new line in dialogue.
options: Keep every speaker in one long paragraph.
Start a new line for the new speaker.
Use brackets instead of speech marks.

cases.prompt: Why is a new line helpful in dialogue?
cases.correct: It shows that the speaker has changed.
cases.explanation: Line breaks support clarity.
options: It shows that the speaker has changed.
It removes the need for punctuation.
It turns a statement into a question.

templates.title: Exclamation mark inside speech marks
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Punctuate: 'Stop shouted the lifeguard.'
cases.explanation: The exclamation mark is part of the spoken words.

cases.prompt: Punctuate: 'Watch out cried Sam.'
cases.explanation: End punctuation belongs inside speech marks.

templates.title: Singular and plural regular possession
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Choose the phrase for one teacher and her desk.
cases.explanation: One teacher owns the desk, so apostrophe before s.

cases.prompt: Choose the phrase for several teachers and their desks.
cases.explanation: Regular plural ending in s takes the apostrophe after s.

templates.title: Irregular plural possession
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Choose the correct phrase for children and their coats.
cases.explanation: Children is plural but does not end in s, so add 's.

cases.prompt: Choose the correct phrase for women and their race.
cases.explanation: Women is an irregular plural.

templates.title: Contraction or possession
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: In 'The dog's barking loudly', what does the apostrophe show?
cases.explanation: It means 'dog is', so letters have been omitted.

cases.prompt: In 'The dog's bowl is empty', what does the apostrophe show?
cases.explanation: The bowl belongs to one dog.

templates.title: Apostrophe meaning contrast
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which phrase means boots belonging to one girl?
cases.explanation: Apostrophe before s shows one owner.

cases.prompt: Which phrase means kits belonging to more than one team?
cases.explanation: Regular plural owner uses apostrophe after s.

templates.title: Semicolon between related clauses
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
cases.correct: The sky darkened; the gulls flew inland.
cases.explanation: A semicolon can join two closely related main clauses.
options: The sky darkened; the gulls flew inland.
The sky; darkened the gulls flew inland.
The sky darkened; and the gulls.
The sky; the gulls; flew inland.

cases.prompt: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
cases.explanation: Both sides can stand as main clauses.

templates.title: Colon for explanation
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
cases.correct: I needed one thing: a torch.
cases.explanation: The first part is a complete clause; the second explains it.
options: I needed: one thing a torch.
I needed one thing: a torch.
I needed one: thing a torch.
I needed one thing a: torch.

cases.prompt: Which sentence uses a colon to introduce a list?
cases.correct: The box contained three tools: a hammer, a saw and a chisel.
cases.explanation: A colon can introduce a list after a complete clause.
options: The box contained three tools: a hammer, a saw and a chisel.
The box contained: three tools a hammer, a saw and a chisel.
The box: contained three tools, a hammer, a saw and a chisel.
The box contained three: tools a hammer.

templates.title: Dash for a strong break
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which sentence uses a dash effectively?
cases.correct: The answer was obvious - nobody had locked the door.
cases.explanation: The dash introduces an explanation.
options: The answer was obvious - nobody had locked the door.
The answer - was obvious nobody had locked the door.
The answer was - obvious nobody had locked the door.
The answer was obvious nobody - had locked the door.

cases.prompt: Which punctuation best completes the sentence? 'I opened the box ___ it was empty.'
cases.explanation: A dash can create a dramatic break before the explanation.

templates.title: Repair comma splices
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which revision fixes the comma splice? 'The rain stopped, we went outside.'
cases.correct: The rain stopped; we went outside.
cases.explanation: Two main clauses need stronger punctuation or a conjunction.
options: The rain stopped, we went outside.
The rain stopped; we went outside.
The rain; stopped, we went outside.
The rain stopped we; went outside.

cases.prompt: Which sentence repairs the boundary? 'The bell rang, the class lined up.'
cases.correct: The bell rang, so the class lined up.
cases.explanation: Adding a conjunction makes the comma work.
options: The bell rang, the class lined up.
The bell rang, so the class lined up.
The bell, rang the class lined up.
The bell rang the class, lined up.

templates.title: Hyphen for compound modifiers
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which phrase clearly means a shark that eats people?
cases.explanation: The hyphen shows the words work together as a modifier.

cases.prompt: Which phrase clearly describes a cake made by a child?
cases.explanation: The hyphen avoids confusion.

templates.title: Meaning changes with hyphens
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which phrase means workers who work part time?
cases.explanation: The hyphen joins 'part' and 'time' as one idea.

cases.prompt: Which phrase means a snake that is eating an egg?
cases.explanation: The hyphen makes the intended modifier clear.

templates.title: Do not usually hyphenate -ly adverbs
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which phrase is usually punctuated best?
cases.explanation: -ly adverbs are usually not hyphenated before adjectives/participles.

cases.prompt: Which option avoids an unnecessary hyphen?
cases.explanation: 'Brightly' is an -ly adverb.

templates.title: Repair ambiguity with a hyphen
templates.rationale: Hand-authored bench-expansion template for KS2 Grammar practice.

cases.prompt: Which version avoids ambiguity?
cases.explanation: The hyphen shows the number twenty-four.

cases.prompt: Which phrase is clearest for a coach who trains athletes?
cases.explanation: The hyphen links the words working as a modifier.
